# The one header a feed file cannot carry

**Generated by `scripts/sync-spec.sh` from the validator package.**
Do not edit — the same words ship in the validator CLI and on
cabuya.org's quickstart, and a hand-edit here would make this the copy
that drifts.

The specification calls `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` **the one
non-obvious MUST** (§3, the feed envelope). It is the check a publisher
who did everything else right fails first: two static files at stable
URLs are schema-valid and are **not** L2, because the header is a
property of the server and no amount of editing JSON produces it.

Without it, every consumer running in a browser needs a server-side
proxy to read the feed — so the participants with the lowest cost to
build are exactly the ones locked out.

The validator reports it as **ENV007**.

| Host | What to add |
|---|---|
| Cloudflare Pages | `_headers` |
| Netlify | `_headers` |
| Vercel | `vercel.json` |
| nginx | *server configuration* |
| Apache | `.htaccess` |
| Amazon S3 + CloudFront | *server configuration* |
| GitHub Pages | *nothing — see below* |

### Cloudflare Pages

A `_headers` file at the root of the published output. Cloudflare applies it at the edge, so nothing in your build has to know about it.

`_headers`:

```
/*
  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

### Netlify

The same `_headers` format, in the publish directory. Netlify ignores the file if it is outside it, which is the usual reason a correct file has no effect.

`_headers`:

```
/*
  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

### Vercel

Merge the `headers` array into an existing `vercel.json` rather than replacing the file.

`vercel.json`:

```
{
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/(.*)",
      "headers": [
        { "key": "Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "value": "*" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

### nginx

Scope it to the manifest and the feeds rather than to the whole server. `add_header` inside a `location` block replaces any inherited headers, so declare it where it applies.

```
location /.well-known/cabuya.json {
  add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin *;
}

location /feeds/ {
  add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin *;
}
```

### Apache

Needs `mod_headers` enabled. On shared hosting it usually is; if the header does not appear, that module is the first thing to check.

`.htaccess`:

```
<FilesMatch "cabuya\.json$|\.json$">
  Header set Access-Control-Allow-Origin "*"
</FilesMatch>
```

### Amazon S3 + CloudFront

The bucket CORS configuration. CloudFront must also be told to forward the `Origin` header, or it caches one response for every origin and the header never varies.

```
{
  "CORSRules": [
    {
      "AllowedOrigins": ["*"],
      "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"],
      "AllowedHeaders": ["*"]
    }
  ]
}
```

### GitHub Pages

GitHub Pages does not let you set response headers, and it already sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response. Nothing to do — but nothing you can do either, if that ever changes.
